newsitem.title: INDIA: India HFCL blames prices for profit fall.
newsitem.headline: India HFCL blames prices for profit fall.

text.p: India's Himachal Futuristic Communications Ltd (HFCL) on Tuesday blamed a sharp fall in its 1996/97 (April-March) net profit on tumbling telecommunications equipment prices.

HFCL's 1996/97 net profit plunged to 165.8 million rupees ($4.6 million) ($4.63 million) from 416.8 million rupees in 1995/96. Its sales fell to 2.0 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 2.43 billion rupees.
But the firm said it expected its net profit in 1997/98 to surge to 500 million rupees on the back of higher sales.

HFCL director Mahendra Nahata told Reuters the fall in profit reflected the drop in purchase prices fixed by the state-owned Department of Telecommunications (DoT), which currently enjoys a monopoly over basic telephone services.
Nahata said DoT's purchase prices for certain items had fallen by more than 40 percent during 1996/97. "In areas such as optical line terminal equipment, the margins have become razor thin," he said.

As the only basic telephone services provider in India, DoT is the main buyer of telecommunications equipment. All Indian telecommunications equipment manufacturers are dependent on DoT purchases for their financial health.
Nahata said he expected HFCL to rebound in 1997/98, and post sales of 3.5 billion rupees, and a net profit of 500 million rupees.
HFCL expects to get one billion rupees of business from DoT in 1997/98, apart from 250 million rupees' worth that it is already implementing, he said.
Nahata added that HFCL had also received orders worth about two billion rupees for turnkey transmission from private service providers.

India auctioned licences for basic telephone services to private operators for 21 zones in 1995 as part of an economic liberalisation programme launched in 1991. The first private operators are expected to start providing services towards the end of 1997.
HFCL hit the headlines in 1995 when it offered a staggering $27 billion for licences to set up basic telephone networks in nine zones.
It is currently engaged in a legal dispute with the Indian government over the financial modalities of the licensing process. The dispute is being heard in Indian courts. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
